articles.fullContent:
Key takeaways

  1. The most important social video metrics include average watch time, engagement rate, video completion rate, play rate, shares, saves, and conversion rate.
  2. Every platform defines a “view” differently, so comparing raw view counts across TikTok, Instagram, YouTube, and LinkedIn without context can be misleading.
  3. The metrics you prioritize should map directly to your goal, whether that’s brand awareness, audience retention, or proving ROI.
  4. Tracking metrics across multiple platforms is easier with a unified analytics tool like Hootsuite Social OS than with native dashboards alone.

What are social video metrics and why do they matter?

Social video metrics are the numbers that show how your video content performs on social media platforms. They track how often your videos are watched, how people interact with them, and what actions viewers take after watching.

At their best, video marketing metrics don’t just tell you what happened, they show you why. These are the insights that help shape smarter content, better social media campaigns, and a stronger connection with your target audience.

Some examples of social video metrics include:

  • View count: How many times your video was played.
  • Watch time: How long people stayed engaged.
  • Engagement rate: How often viewers interacted (likes, comments, shares).
  • Video completion rate: How many viewers watched all the way through.
  • Play rate: What share of people who saw your video actually pressed play.
  • Click-through rate (CTR): How often viewers clicked on your call-to-action (CTA).
  • Shares and saves: Indicators of content that resonates and drives social sharing.

These metrics matter because they’re how you measure the actual impact of your video strategy. They help you understand what’s working (and what’s not), refine your creative and messaging, and compare performance across social channels.

They also matter upward. When roughly $1 of every $5 in digital ads goes to social video, metrics are the bridge between creative work and business outcomes, especially when you need to defend video budget or justify headcount. A clean set of numbers tied to revenue, pipeline, or reach is what turns a quarterly report into buy-in. Pulling those numbers from social media analytics tools makes that reporting far less painful than stitching together screenshots from six dashboards.

Bonus: Get a free social media analytics report template  that shows you the most important metrics to track for each network.

Which social video metrics should you track?

The video metrics you should track depend entirely on your goals. For example, what you’d measure for a brand awareness campaign looks completely different from what you’d measure for a community-building one.

Before you dive into the full list, here’s the short version of how social media video KPIs map to common goals:

  • Awareness goals: Lean on reach-based metrics like views and impressions.
  • Attention goals: Lean on watch time, completion rate, and retention.
  • Revenue goals: Lean on CTR, conversion rate, and traffic source.

Here’s a fuller guide to which metrics to track based on your goal:

Our advice? Pick two or three KPIs that align with your goal, and don’t get distracted by the rest.

11 top social video metrics to track (and why they matter)

Here are the top social video metrics that can tell you the most about your performance across all channels.

1. View count

View count tells you how many times your video has been watched. But don’t let that simplicity fool you. Views are still one of the most important video metrics, especially for measuring brand awareness and reach.

Every platform defines a “view” differently, so context matters.

Here’s what counts as a view by platform:

  • Facebook:

    • Reel: The moment the video starts playing

    • In-feed video: 3 seconds or more

  • Instagram:

    • Reel: The moment the video starts playing (including replays)

    • In-feed video: 3 seconds or more

  • YouTube:

    • Video: 30 seconds or more

    • Shorts: The moment your video starts playing. Note: this means even if a user scrolls past, it counts as a view as long as the video begins to play.

  • TikTok: 1 second (or 3 seconds for videos 3 minutes and longer)
  • LinkedIn: 2 seconds or more, with at least 50% of the video on screen
  • X (Twitter): 2 seconds or more, with at least 50% of the video on screen
  • Snapchat: 1 second or more for organic Stories (Snap Ads count a video view at 2 seconds)

articles.title: Why social-first AI wins where general AI fails in 2026
articles.fullContent:
Key takeaways

  1. Social-first AI is AI designed specifically for social media, using real-time social data rather than static web content to power insights, content, and trend detection.
  2. Most general-purpose AI tools are adding work, not saving it, with 43% of social media managers spending 11+ hours a week on AI tools.
  3. Only 28% of social media managers are confident their tools reflect what’s happening on social right now, which forces constant oversight and edits.
  4. Hootsuite Social OS is built as a social-first AI system, connecting real-time intelligence (Lumen), content creation (Perch), and AI orchestration (Wisdom) in governed workflows.

What is social-first AI?

Social-first AI is artificial intelligence designed around social media data and social media workflows. Instead of drawing on general web crawls with a training cutoff, it works from live signals across social platforms, so the insights and content it produces reflect what people are talking about now.

The distinction matters because social moves differently from almost every other marketing channel. A trend can form and fade inside 48 hours. Tone shifts by platform, by audience, and sometimes by week. General-purpose AI for social media tends to flatten all of that into something safe, generic, and slightly out of date.

Most social-first AI systems share a few defining characteristics:

  • Real-time data foundation: Insights come from live social conversations, not static training data with a knowledge cutoff.
  • Platform-native understanding: It recognizes that a LinkedIn post, a TikTok hook, and an Instagram caption are different jobs with different norms.
  • Proactive trend detection: It surfaces emerging topics while there’s still time to act, rather than summarizing what already happened.
  • Social-specific tone and context: Outputs reflect how people actually talk online, including the references and formats native to each channel.
  • Governed outputs: Answers are traceable to sources, and content moves through approval workflows before it goes live.

Put simply, social-first AI treats social as the primary data source and the primary workflow, not an afterthought bolted onto a general marketing tool.

How does social-first AI compare to general-purpose AI?

The clearest way to see the difference is side by side. Both approaches use large language models, but what they’re grounded in, and what they’re optimized for, diverges sharply.

The core difference comes down to grounding. General-purpose social media AI tools are strong at language and weak at timing. Social-first AI is built so that timing, tone, and platform context are part of the answer, not something your team has to add afterward.

Why does general-purpose AI fail social teams?

General-purpose AI fails social teams because it wasn’t designed for the pace or style of modern social. The problem isn’t that AI lacks potential, or that its underlying algorithms are flawed.

These tools promise automation but require micromanagement. This is unsurprising when only 16% of marketing work is currently AI-automated. They surface information but lack context, and they’re trained on data that rarely reflects what people care about right now.

If we zoom out more, a clear disconnect emerges between how leaders think AI is performing and how it’s actually landing on the front lines. 64% of senior marketers believe their tools use real-time data, but only 39% of social media managers agree.

Marketing leaders are far more confident in their AI’s real-time data than the practitioners using it daily.

As AI budgets rise and expectations grow, the cracks are starting to show. The people closest to the work, closest to the platforms, the conversations, and the trends, know the truth: most AI-powered tools can’t keep up.

And when your tools can’t keep up, neither can your team. Instead of solving problems, most AI-driven tools are actually creating more work for already busy social teams. Here are three reasons AI is falling short, and what needs to change for social strategies to actually benefit.

Is AI actually saving social teams time?

For most teams, no. AI is adding hours rather than saving them. It was pitched as the time-saver social teams have been waiting for, but in practice, it’s become a big time sink.

43% of social media managers now spend more than 11 hours a week using AI tools. That’s a full third of their time spent coaxing content out of tools that were supposed to eliminate busywork.

Key Takeaways

  • Trending Keywords is a new section in AnswerThePublic that shows the searches whose interest is growing fastest around your keyword over the last 30 days.
  • It lives in two places: the Web report (Google search trends, directly under Top Organic Searches) and the YouTube report (labeled “Trending Keywords · YouTube”).

A keyword shows up in your research tool with a clean volume number next to it. You write the article. You publish it. And it lands on a results page that already has a dozen strong pages on it, because everyone else’s tool showed them the same number around the same time.

That is the problem with researching only what people have already searched. By the time a keyword has volume you can point to, the early window has usually closed. The people who won it were writing while the number was still small and the direction was obvious.

AnswerThePublic built Trending Keywords for that window. It shows the searches growing fastest around your topic in the last 30 days, on Google and on YouTube, so you can see a rise while it is still a rise.

What Are Trending Keywords in AnswerThePublic?

Trending Keywords is a section in the AnswerThePublic report that lists the searches whose interest is growing fastest around the keyword you entered, over the last 30 days. The data comes from Google Trends, and each section carries an “Updated today” label.

It sits next to the data you already use. The classic question wheel still shows what people ask. Top Organic Searches still shows what they search today. Trending Keywords adds the direction: what is picking up speed right now.

You will find it in two reports, and each one answers a different question.

Where Does Trending Keywords Show Up in the Web Report?

In the Web report, Trending Keywords appears as a new section directly under Top Organic Searches, with a NEW badge next to the title. It shows the Google searches rising fastest around your keyword over the last 30 days.

Read it as a second layer under Top Organic Searches. The list above shows what the top of the results already looks like. The list below shows what is climbing toward it.

The table has three columns:

  • Keywords: the rising search itself.
  • Search Increase: how much interest has grown over the 30 days, shown as a percentage. You can sort the list by it.
  • Search Interest: a bar showing how much interest the search has right now.

The section shows the top 5 rows, and a “View results” button opens the full list.

Each row has a plus icon on the left. Click it and a small menu opens with two options: Copy and Generate Content. Copy gives you the keyword to drop into a spreadsheet, a brief, or a message to your writer. Generate Content sends it to AnswerThePublic Content Studio.

This one is for anyone who plans video. YouTube is a search destination of its own, and the topics rising there do not always match what is rising in Google’s results. A creator who checks only the Web report can miss a topic that is already taking off in video.

Here is what that looks like in practice.

In a sample search for “content creation,” the YouTube section listed rising searches such as “ai songs,” “remote work,” “personal branding,” “trending education,” and “vr content creation.” One row in that screenshot showed a Search Increase of +81,800%.

What Does a BREAKOUT Tag Mean?

articles.title: Ticker: Carson Daly Named Saturday Today Co-Anchor
articles.fullContent:
By Mark Mwachiro Top of the Ticker: NBC News has named Carson Daly the co-anchor of Saturday Today, beginning Saturday, November 7. Daly will continue his weekday role, expanding his duties at NBC News to six days a week.

“I’m thrilled to add Saturday Today to my weekday morning schedule,” said Daly, who will join co-anchor Laura Jarrett , feature anchor Joe Fryer , and meteorologist Angie Lassman .

Daly, who joined Today as host of the Orange Room in 2013, fills the void left by Peter Alexander , who left the program in March and later left NBC News after more than 20 years to join MS NOW .

Revolving Door: CNBC announced it has signed a new long-term agreement with Jim Cramer , which includes launching a premium subscription tier of his CNBC Investing Club in 2027.

The business network also recently announced some executive moves affecting its dayside programming and editorial operations.

Vice president of programming and senior executive producer Todd Bonin will now lead Business Day from 5 a.m. to noon ET. Sandy Cannold , vp of programming and sep will now oversee the network’s programming from noon to 6 p.m. ET.

Meanwhile, Jason Gewirtz moves to the Digital Control Room, while Anne Tironi will continue to oversee Squawk Box and Lisa Villalobos will manage all three hours of Squawk on the Street. Both will report to Bonin. In addition to leading Closing Bell: Overtime, Maria Boden will take on Fast Money. Matt Quayle will move from sep of The Exchange and Power Lunch to a new role focused on content development across platforms.

On the newsgathering and reporting front, Lacy O’Toole , vp and managing editor, will also add the network’s Specials unit to her docket. All correspondents will now report directly to O’Toole, except those aligned with the strategic verticals led by Max Meyers . In addition, correspondents based in Washington, D.C. and San Francisco will report to MC Wellons and Christina Passariello , respectively. Finally, CNBC’s Investigations unit will fall under the purview of Ken Brown , with Scott Zamost and Paige Tortorelli reporting to him.

Brand refresh : MS NOW has introduced a new brand campaign titled “Now There’s More That Unites US.” The network says this campaign was inspired by “the groundswell of participation, with millions of individuals making their voices heard, standing up for what they believe in.”

Members will be able to watch MS NOW’s 24/7 live linear feed on a TV without a cable subscription, and can also watch full episodes of all of MS NOW’s programs, available on demand.

Stork deliveries : Fox News’ Peter Doocy and CNN’s Abby Phillip recently welcomed new additions to their respective families. Doocy welcomed his third child, Molly Kate Doocy , on October 22. Phillip welcomed her second child, Maxwell Elias Richardson , a late-October surprise born on Oct. 27.

articles.title: #AskNewser: CNN, NBC News and NewsNation Executives Reflect on Their Election Night Coverage
articles.fullContent:
By Mark Mwachiro As the dust settles from a historic midterm election that saw the Democratic Party surf a blue wave to capture both the Senate and the House, news outlets are downshifting from special coverage and settling back into regular programming.

With 31 million viewers tuning in Tuesday night across 13 networks, TVNewser recently spoke to NBC News’ evp, creative, innovation & field production Marc Greenstein , whose network was the No.1 network during primetime in total viewers and the Adults 25-54 demo, as well as CNN’s svp, Washington & special events programming Abigail Crutchfield , whose network was the most-watched cable news network in the prized demo, and NewsNation’s political director Chris Stirewalt , whose network in coordination with Decision Desk HQ was the first one to call both the House and the Senate for the Democrats, for a post-election AskNewser on what worked well during their live election coverage.

TVNewser: What worked well from a coverage and technology standpoint on election night?

Greenstein : Steve Kornacki continues to be the best at breaking down the vote, providing context and helping viewers understand not just what is happening, but where the night is headed.

We combined editorial and technology in a new way, allowing Steve to contribute to the linear broadcast while simultaneously hosting his own dedicated streaming feed from the same studio as Savannah Guthrie and Tom Llamas . This allowed us to produce two distinct broadcasts just feet apart, each tailored to its audience, without losing the editorial connection between our talent.

Extensive planning for multiple election scenarios allowed us to react quickly as race calls came in. We deployed multiple correspondents across nearly every battleground state, covering both voting developments and candidate headquarters. This gave us a strong presence in the places driving the story and allowed us to bring firsthand reporting and reaction into the broadcast throughout the night.

We played more than 35,000 graphics across our zones and platforms, delivering results and analysis with speed and clarity. We brought together broadcast, streaming and digital coverage under a consistent editorial and visual approach, while tailoring the experience to each platform. The launch of our dedicated vertical video feed was another important step in reaching audiences in new ways without compromising the depth or quality of our journalism.

Cruthchfield : It was having all of our experts and talent together in one place. It gave the DC bureau great energy, and it was fun to watch the reporters and anchors work together to unpack the results.

Our director, Reza Baktar , designed a phenomenal set that gave us more mobility than ever and made it easy to get to any data set we needed at any moment. I also loved giving John King the ability to analyze the data at the magic wall or to bring his mini magic wall over to our analyst tables to be a part of the conversation. And I loved King’s new vertical magic wall, which opened up new storytelling options.

Stirewalt : You can’t beat the cards. We had such an advantage by having Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ) on our side. I think we did a good job of bringing viewers into the process and explaining what we were doing, but when you get down to it, the advantage of being so far ahead of the competition was just amazing.

TN: What was the biggest surprise of the night?

Greenstein : The biggest surprise was how quickly we were able to call control of the Senate. While there was a general sense that it could be a good night for Democrats, I think the early call caught many of us a little off guard. That said, we had planned for a wide range of scenarios and were prepared to stay on air throughout the night across the broadcast network, NBC News Now and Kornacki Cam.

Another pleasant surprise was how well the AI audio technology worked, allowing us to produce the linear and streaming broadcasts simultaneously from the same studio. We had limited time to rehearse with the technology, so there were certainly some nerves heading into the night. But it performed remarkably well and allowed us to pull off something we had never done before.

Cruthchfield : I think perhaps how quickly we were able to project the major results of the night. We always plan for every scenario, but this Tuesday we got answers from the voters quickly.

Stirewalt : How much work I wasted preparing for close elections in so many places. I was buckled in for tight contests in battleground states. We found out by 8:30 p.m. ET or so that what we really needed to get good at was going deep on places like Mississippi.

TN: Share the tricks you used to keep yourself awake and alert on Tuesday night.

Greenstein : Coffee, Diet Coke, and the adrenaline of being in the director’s chair! In my role, I rarely get the opportunity to direct. The last time was Election Night 2024. So getting back in the chair and working alongside the most talented people in the business, both on air and behind the scenes, pushes me to be at the top of my game. And I love every minute of it.

Cruthchfield : A lot of hot tea, a phenomenal team, and a big bag of gummy bears.

Stirewalt : I don’t need any outside stimulants. When the results started pouring in, I was so thrilled at how DDHQ and our team were doing that I was just high on life.

Mark Mwachiro is a TVNewser contributor who has been writing for the blog since March 2022. Based out of New York, Mark has also contributed to ADWEEK.

articles.title: Fox Corp. Completes $22 Billion Deal for Roku
articles.fullContent:
By Mark Mwachiro There is a new sheriff in Roku City: Fox has completed its purchase of the streaming and tech company.

The $22 billion deal closed today, combining Fox Corp.’s broadcast, news, sports, streaming, and local news portfolio with Roku’s open connected TV platform and first-party data from more than 100 million global streaming households.

The merged company becomes the third-largest entity in U.S. television by share of viewing. Fox says the addition of Roku will create new opportunities to serve its viewers, advertisers, and partners.

Executive chair and CEO of Fox Corp. Lachlan Murdoch said acquiring Roku advances the media company’s long-term strategy and will continue to “relentlessly serve audiences and partners, while reinforcing the openness and choice that is the essence of the Roku platform.”

Roku will be folded into Fox Digital Platforms, which also houses fellow FAST service Tubi, Fox One, and Red Seat Ventures. The streaming platform’s founder, Anthony Wood, will join Fox’s board of directors and serve as co-chair of Fox Digital Platforms alongside Paul Cheesbrough, the unit’s CEO.

When the merger was announced in June , the companies said they were looking to create a “scaled next-generation media and technology company” to prosper in today’s environment of increasing consumption of live sports, news, and streaming.

Roku stockholders will receive $95.30 in cash and 0.9799 shares of Fox Class A common stock for each share of Roku Class A and Roku Class B common stock they owned before the deal closed, under the merger agreement.

Separately, Fox shareholders will now own approximately 74% of the outstanding shares of Fox common stock, and the remaining approximately 26% will go to former Roku shareholders.

Reflecting on Roku’s acquisition, Woods said in a statement that he was proud of what his team has built and that combining with Fox provides an opportunity to accelerate its vision, scale faster, and be more aggressive in innovation for its respective audiences.

Woods added, “I couldn’t be more excited about what we’ll accomplish together.”

Mark Mwachiro is a TVNewser contributor who has been writing for the blog since March 2022. Based out of New York, Mark has also contributed to ADWEEK.

articles.title: Meerkat’s Dustin Black Makes an Art of Staying Curious
articles.fullContent:
By Eva Kis Creative energy doesn’t ebb when the world stops. So when the pandemic stalled agency work in 2020, Dustin Black turned his lifelong pursuit of creativity on his home.

The career art director—recently named chief creative officer and partner at full-service Minneapolis creative agency Meerkat (formerly Preston Spire)—has twin daughters, who were 6 years old at the time. He’d been planning to turn their family mantra—“Be brave, be curious, be kind”—into a giant banner for their home, and suddenly had the time to make it.

Using felt sourced from New York-based manufacturer Oxford Pennant , Black’s banner infused some much-needed cheer into their basement. He also shared the finished product with the company.

“Oxford Pennant just absolutely loved it,” he said, so much so that they began producing a pennant using Black’s design—and offered him a supply of felt for future projects.

In fact, Black did have another idea in the works: He’d been sculpting a 5-foot-long fish out of foam that was in need of scales. As it happened, at-home cutting machine maker Cricut had also taken an interest in Black’s banner and offered to sponsor his work.

All that was left was for Black to take every hands-on art lesson, from fingerpainting as a toddler to his double major in art at the University of Nebraska-Lincoln, and apply it to a new kind of blank slate. “I had to figure out, what would a felt fish look like? I started playing, and I suddenly had my first fish covered in felt scales,” he said.

Black has been chasing new creative highs ever since, from making ever-more complex scales to cladding his fish in felt flowers instead, then turning to sculpting birds. Each sculpture begins with elaborate sketches, then Black figures out the size and frames it out in metal, wood, and foam.

The Cricut does the tedious work of cutting out the felt, then Black glues on each piece and further decorates it with paint and other materials. Everything is done inside his 25-square-foot home office on nights and weekends.

The ‘Bizarre Chemistry’ of Card Collecting With Fuse Create’s Grant Cleland Since the beginning, he’s involved his girls to “show them it’s OK to try something new and fail” (they now have their own art projects as well). Black also documents the creative process of each piece on Instagram, including his mistakes and how he moved on from them.

“I’m trying to put out there the notion of we’re all beginners, and we’re all figuring it out, and it might look good in the end but it took a lot to get there,” he explained.

His sculptures have been exhibited in galleries, at events and, most recently, for a year at Minneapolis-Saint Paul International Airport. Having them in a public space “has been a lot of fun because I get random texts from people: ‘Look at what my family group chat is talking about!’” he said.

The pursuit of new shapes, styles, and designs is what drives Black, which is why he’s resisted taking commissions that would dictate what he makes—or worse, copy his previous work.

His latest project, an eagle with feathers made of polymer clay that Black hand-painted, has pride of place inside the Meerkat offices. With the widespread suspicion of AI in creative work, Black knows the value in clients being able to see and touch a piece of art made in-house.

He also hopes it inspires the kind of creativity that drives good work: “We need to be doing new things. We need to be solving complex problems. And we need to use curiosity to approach it.”

articles.title: Brandweek 2026: The ‘Why’ Test Behind Mars’ Boldest Ideas ft. Rankin Carroll
articles.fullContent:
By Jenny Rooney The best creative risks should make you a little nervous. But they should never make you ask why your brand is taking them.

Live from the Marketing Vanguard stage at Brandweek 2026 , Jenny Rooney sits down with Rankin Carroll, chief brand officer of Mars Snacking, to unpack how brands like M&M’s, Snickers and Skittles stay culturally relevant without treating boldness as an excuse for chaos.

Rankin takes us behind the scenes of the 2023 Snickers AI experiment that felt “potentially crazy” at the time.

He also gets candid about Mars’ creator learning curve and the responsibility marketers have to the next generation.

How Mars pressure-tests risky ideas before putting iconic brands on the line

Why the 2023 Snickers AI experiment required legal, security and agency teams to take the risk together

How “Why us? Why this brand?” separates bold creative from stunts

Why brands have to earn the credibility to participate authentically in culture

Why Rankin believes transformation now has no end state

How Mars is learning to loosen control in creator-led marketing

Why marketing leaders need to rethink how the next generation is trained for an AI-shaped industry

Why CMOs need to own the AI agenda instead of leaving it to scattered pilots

This episode is part of a special vidcast series that was recorded live during Brandweek 2026 and presented in partnership with Tatari.

Rankin Carroll is Chief Brand Officer of Mars Snacking, where he works across some of the company’s most recognizable brands, including M&M’s, Snickers and Skittles. He has spent more than 20 years at Mars across marketing, advertising, general management and global and regional leadership roles. His career has taken him from Toronto to the UK and at one point, included running an ice cream business along the way.

Today, Rankin focuses on what he describes as the stewardship of distinctive, iconic brands: protect what makes them valuable, make them stronger than when you received them, and still create enough tension to keep them culturally relevant.

[04:33] The Snickers AI Bet That Looked “Potentially Crazy” — In 2023, Mars put Snickers into an agentic creative experience at a point when the safety and reputational risks looked far less understood than they do today. The project involved roughly ten tech partners, legal and security leadership, and a list of 8,000 blocked words. The takeaway is much bigger than “take more risk.” It’s that ambitious experimentation becomes possible when the organization commits to solving the risk together.

[07:56] Earn the Right to Take Risks — Rankin draws a hard line between calculated cultural risk and performative brand behavior. Skittles could maintain its relationship with the LGBTQ+ community during a more volatile period because the brand had spent years building credibility there. His filter for every big swing is simple: Why us? Why this brand? If there is no strategically convincing answer, the idea does not deserve the risk.

[13:42] Are We Preparing the Next Generation for What Marketing Becomes Next? — Rankin raises one of the more uncomfortable questions from Brandweek 2026: what happens to junior marketers when the profession changes around AI? He expects the practice to look completely different within three years and openly says he does not yet have a satisfying answer for how marketers entering the industry should be trained. For him, that makes talent development a leadership responsibility, not an HR afterthought.

[15:03] “A Thousand Pilots and No Progress” — Rankin believes leaving AI adoption to disconnected enthusiasts across an organization is a recipe for chaos. CMOs need to own the agenda alongside technology leadership, bringing top-down clarity to investment, priorities and what the company should build, buy, rent or borrow. His warning is simple: just because you can use AI somewhere does not mean you should.

Jenny Rooney is Chief Brand and Community Officer, leading strategy for the overall ADWEEK brand as well as the ways in which we serve and support our audiences with high-value content, products, partnerships and experiences, notably through our community programs such as Marketing Vanguard.

articles.title: Political Campaigns Spent a Near-Record $331 Per Voter, But Waste Forces Rethink
articles.fullContent:
Maine, Alaska, and Iowa saw campaign spending surge to between $252 and $331 per registered voter.

Republicans outspent Democrats in battlegrounds but still lost key races in four of five states.

Despite money moving to CTV and digital, targeting misfires included an Ohio 8-year-old being served attack ads on YouTube.

Beta · Generated by AI, reviewed by ADWEEK newsroom Where are the most expensive media markets in the U.S.? At least for political campaigns in 2026, they were Maine, Alaska, and Iowa.

These thinly populated battleground states saw spending of up to $331 per registered voter for the 2026 election cycle, according to data from AdImpact and state voter rolls.

That came as total political spending hit a record $11.9 billion across TV, digital, and audio, exceeding the 2024 presidential year’s $11.2 billion. None of that includes substantial direct mail or outdoor campaigns.

Maine saw the highest spending per voter at $331, followed by Alaska at $313 and Iowa at $252. They fell just shy of a record set by Montana in 2024, which got $335 per voter thanks to a competitive Senate seat. Competitive Senate and gubernatorial races fueled a record number of three-digit outlays per voter in 2026, including Ohio ($112) and Kansas ($102).

Spending per voter doubled and even tripled from two years ago in all five triple-digit-spending states. Republicans outspent Democrats in four of those five but lost key races in all of them, per AdImpact, with the Alaska Senate race still being counted.

That so much money failed to change outcomes could force a major rethink of 2028 strategy.

The Four Down and Dirtiest Political Ads of the 2026 Midterms Targeting misfires

Heavy spending meant local ads spilling into national buys. By October, Senate campaign ads from Iowa, Texas, Florida, Maine, and Kansas ran on some national broadcasts of NCAA and NFL football games.

A shift to digital and connected TV spending this year made targeting theoretically easier, but didn’t guarantee reaching the right people.

Sal Tuzzeo, a Fabric Media executive based near Cleveland, said his 8-year-old son was bombarded by political ads, even though he was watching age-appropriate content on the big screen from YouTube creators TerraGreen , The Fish Guys , and Unspeakable .

“The amount of political money flowing into streaming and CTV seemed absurd,” Tuzzeo said. “The mistargeting was egregious.” He attributed it to “a broad reach land grab coupled with overt aversion to frequency capping.”

Over the past few months, nearly every ad in every pod his son watched was political, Tuzzeo said. His child could recite verbatim ads dealing with abortion, sex changes, crack cocaine, and domestic violence.

Republicans outspent Democrats by a $5.5 billion to $5 billion margin nationwide, per AdImpact. But that advantage made little difference. For example, of 87 candidates backed by Elon Musk’s America PAC, 80 lost, according to Travis Trawick, CEO of nonpartisan election tech firm FullPAC.

Too much money went into broadcast over the final five weeks, when time is most expensive and when “at least in this election, most people’s minds were already made up,” Trawick said. “Running the same ad in front of people 60 times just has diminishing returns.”

For 2028, he believes campaigns will shift spending earlier in the cycle and toward AI-driven digital and social strategies, using AI not just to optimize media but also to collect return path signals and shape creative that spawns voter engagement.

“Being able to create a conversation between a voter and a candidate or an issue, not just talking at them, and doing that at scale, is something that’s never really been possible before,” Trawick said. “Now it is.”

What is content moderation?

Content moderation is the process of reviewing, filtering, and responding to comments, messages, and other user-generated content on your social channels.

articles.title: Google Explains How Redirects Affect Ranking Signals via @sejournal, @martinibuster
articles.fullContent:
Google’s Gary Illyes and Cherry Prommawin discussed how permanent and temporary redirects affect canonicalization and ranking signals. They explained that both can help Google recognize related URLs but that they also signal different intentions about which URL should represent the content in Search.

One of the first things they did was to set the table and explain the difference between a 301 and 302 redirect.

A 301 redirect tells the crawler that a change in the URL is permanent and that the search index should be updated with the new URL.

A 302 redirect tells a crawler that a URL change is temporary and that the old URL will eventually be restored.

A Page Will Be Indexed Regardless Of Which Redirect Is Used

Google’s Cherry Prommawin started off the discussion by stating that regardless of what redirect is used, a web page is still going to be indexed by Google. She then affirmed that there are correct choices.

“First of all, relax. No matter which redirect you choose, one of your pages will stay in search and be part of AI training.

There are technically correct choices, but getting it wrong is not the end of the world. Google will still index a page. It’s really just a matter of which URL will show up.”

“Does Google actually care if both numbers, 301, 302, successfully take user to the new page anyway? Aren’t they basically doing the same job?”

“Well, yes and no. Google’s crawlers don’t care at all.”

The conversation next turns to deduplication which is the part where Google groups together similar pages then chooses one page as the one to represent all of the other similar pages in the search index.

“But we have to talk about the real battlefield here, the deduplication process.”

“Ah, the digital family reunion. This is where we look at a room full of identical siblings and try to organize them into a single happy family.

…So in search deduplication, our system have to group all pages with similar main content together. That’s clustering.”

Prommawin added that both 301 and 302 will have an effect on clustering similar pages together. But that only the 301 redirect will have a canonicalization effect.

…then our index has to select just one official URL to represent this entire flock in the search results. Basically, within a cluster, we choose one representative page.

The final selection process is called canonicalization.”

Illyes and Prommawin said that Google has a system for dealing with content that is very similar. Rather than rank no pages from a site, Google will choose to rank one page in a process called deduplication and the page that’s chosen to be representative of all the similar pages is called the canonical.

Some SEOs have this idea called content cannibalization. It’s a concept that began in the early 2000s to explain why pages weren’t getting indexed. The idea is that a group of pages are so similar that Google is choosing not to rank any of them because all of the ranking signals are diluted across all of the URLs with similar content.

But content cannibalization contradicts what we know as a fact about how Google treats similar content in the real world. Google clusters them and then chooses one as the canonical and transfers all of the ranking signals to that one URL.

What SEOs call “cannibalization” is really some other problem like a lack of uniqueness, thin content, and all the other real reasons that cause Google to not index a web page.

301 (permanent) redirect will transfer ranking signals from the old URL to the new URL.

Google will not transfer ranking signals when it encounters a 302 (temporary) redirect.

With a 301 redirect the ranking signals from the old page/pages will transfer to the new URL which will then be the canonical.

Gary explained how the 301 redirect works:

“Google takes all the ranking signals of the old page and hands them to the new page.”

Then he explained why the 302 does not transfer ranking signals:

“Google assumes you are going back eventually, keeps the old URL in the search results, and basically ignores the new URL.”

So if you use a 302 redirect then the new URL will be “basically” ignored by Google.

articles.title: How to add alt text to social media images fast
articles.fullContent:
Social media alt text is easy to skip and expensive to skip as well. Skip it, and you lose the readers who browse with a screen reader. You weaken your content’s chances of surfacing in search. And you fall short of a social media accessibility standard your customers now expect brands to meet.

You don’t have to choose between doing it right and doing it fast. This guide will explain what alt text is, why it matters and how to write it well. We’ll also show you the one-click way to write alt text for social media images at scale.

Sprout Social’s Essentials plan lets you quickly add alt text to your social media images. Open the image in Compose, click Add Alt Text, write a description and save. Or Sprout’s AI Assist analyzes your image and drafts alt text in one click for you to review, edit and publish.

What is alt text on social media?

Alt text, short for alternative text, on social media is a written description attached to an image so screen readers can describe it to people who can’t see or load it.

It fills in what a visual would communicate on its own. People with low vision or those browsing with images turned off still understand your complete post.

Alt text is not a post caption. It’s not a place for commentary, image credits, keywords or calls-to-action. Those add noise for people using screen readers. If the text doesn’t describe what’s in the image, it doesn’t belong in the alt text field.

Facebook, Instagram, LinkedIn, X, Threads and Pinterest all support native alt text fields. Type alt text on each app as you post, or add it across multiple networks in one pass using a publishing platform like Sprout Social.

Why does alt text matter for social media marketers?

Alt text puts your message in front of more people, including those who can’t see the visuals. Adding alt text also makes accessibility a regular part of your publishing routine, which builds credibility and strengthens your brand image.

Does alt text improve accessibility?

Yes. Accessibility is the primary purpose of alt text.

The World Health Organization estimates that 1.3 billion people live with a significant disability. Many use screen readers to turn content into speech or braille. Alt text gives them the information, humor, emotion and context your visual carries.

Alt text also supports people on slow connections or who turn images off to save data. When an image doesn’t load, its description still tells what you shared.

Can alt text help with social media SEO?

Alt text supports social media SEO when it includes words that accurately describe the image and matter to your audience. When it’s written to please an algorithm, it fails the accessibility test and rarely boosts your ranking.

For example, “Three ceramic planters on a white shelf” includes “ceramic planters,” a term your audience may already search. It also gives social platforms more context to surface your content than:

  • “Our latest collection” (too generic)
  • “Best ceramic planters pots sale free shipping” (irrelevant keyword stuffing)

Describe the image accurately, and include the terms that belong there anyway. Discoverability follows.

Is alt text required by policy?

Alt text may be required by your organization’s accessibility policy or applicable laws, depending on your industry, location and audience. Check which requirements apply to your brand.

Even when it’s not mandatory, people expect accessible content from brands. Major social networks also offer tools and accessibility guidance to help.

Adding alt text alone doesn’t guarantee legal compliance. Add it to your publishing checklist alongside captions, transcripts, strong color contrast and clear link text.

What are alt text best practices for social media images?

Good alt text gives people enough detail to understand the image without a long description. Here’s how to keep yours useful:

  • Keep it short but descriptive. Aim for 125 characters as a common guideline. Go longer when the image needs extra explanation.
  • Skip “image of” or “picture of.” Screen readers already announce that an image is present. Start with the description and save your readers the redundancy.
  • Weave in keywords naturally. Include relevant terms only when they describe what’s in the image. Skip search phrases that add nothing to the description.
  • Add context around your visual. When it makes sense, explain why the image is paired with the post. For example, “A line graph showing customer response time falling from six hours to two” is more useful than “A blue line graph.”
  • Leave out hidden messages, credits and calls to action. These distract from the description. Put them in your caption, where everyone can access them.

How long can alt text be on each network?

HTML doesn’t set a character limit for alt text, but social networks and publishing tools do. For example, X allows up to 1,000 characters while Pinterest allows 500. LinkedIn’s publishing API allows up to 4,086 characters but recommends staying under 120.

If you’re publishing through Sprout Social, the following limits apply:

Network Character limit X, Facebook, Instagram, LinkedIn Up to 1,000 Pinterest Up to 500

You don’t need to use all that space. We suggest around 125 characters as a general guideline. Go longer when readers need more detail to understand the image.

How do you add alt text to social media images manually?

Add alt text to your social media images from the same Sprout Compose window you use to draft the rest of your content.

First, log in to your Sprout Social account. New to Sprout? Sign up here and connect your social profiles. Then follow the steps below:

  1. Go to Compose and select the profile(s) you’re publishing to.
  2. Attach an image to your post.
  3. Click the pencil icon on the image.
  4. Click Add Alt Text.
  5. Write your description within the network’s character limit.
  6. Click Save.

An alt text indicator will appear on the image in both Compose and your Publishing Calendar.

Manually adding alt text works. But writing every description from scratch, one image and one post at a time, is where the hours begin to add up.

Why is manual alt text a time drain for growing brands?

Manual alt text takes time because every social media image needs an accurate and relevant description. As your publishing calendar grows, so does the work of writing, checking and adding those descriptions.

If you post images daily across four or five networks, you have dozens of alt text fields to fill each week. Carousels multiply the work, since each image needs its own description.

The work is worth doing. The hours are not. Every minute you spend typing descriptions is time you can’t spend on strategic campaign planning and community management.

articles.fullContent:
Key Takeaways

  • An XML sitemap should include the canonical URLs you want search engines to crawl and index, not every URL on your site.
  • Dynamic sitemaps are the best choice for most websites because they update automatically as pages are added, removed, redirected, or changed.
  • Keep <lastmod> dates accurate and reserve them for meaningful page updates so search engines learn to trust the signal.
  • Google ignores the <changefreq> and <priority> tags, so there’s no SEO benefit to including them.
  • Google Search Console can turn your sitemap into a diagnostic tool by showing which submitted URLs are being discovered and indexed.

Most websites have an XML sitemap. A lot of those sitemaps aren’t optimized, though. 

That means site owners are missing a golden opportunity to improve their SEO and gain an edge over competing brands.

Your sitemap gives search engines a roadmap to the content you want them to find. When that roadmap is full of redirects, non-canonical URLs, or outdated content, search engines have a tougher time doing their jobs.

This forces them to spend time sorting through URLs you don’t really want them to index.

A well-optimized sitemap, on the other hand, gives search engines a more direct path to your most important content. It helps new and updated pages get discovered sooner and keeps search engines focused on the pages you most want them to crawl and index.

In this guide, we’ll look at what belongs in your sitemap and what doesn’t. I’ll also show you how to structure your sitemap to help search engines crawl your site more efficiently.

What Is an XML Sitemap?

In simple terms, an XML sitemap is a file that lists the URLs you want search engines to know about. Think of it as a table of contents that helps crawlers understand what content is available on your site.

    (“XML” stands for “Extensible Markup Language,” a way of structuring and sharing information.)

    A sitemap gives crawlers a direct path to important URLs, so they don’t have to rely entirely on links to discover them. This is especially useful when important pages sit deep within your site or aren’t well connected through your internal linking.

    AI and LLM crawlers can also reference your sitemaps when discovering URLs, turning an optimized sitemap into yet another way to help your content get discovered by AI platforms alongside Google and Bing.

    A basic sitemap entry only needs to provide a few useful pieces of information:

    • Where the page is located: <loc>https://www.example.com/mypage</loc>
    • When it was last significantly updated: <lastmod>2026-09-30</lastmod>

    You may have seen <changefreq> and <priority> in older sitemap examples. Google ignores both, so there’s no reason to include them these days.

    Having a sitemap is only the starting point. If it’s filled with outdated or redirected URLs, you’re not getting nearly as much value from it as you could. So, let’s look at how to optimize it.

    Dynamic vs. Static Sitemaps: Which Should You Use?

    Two types of sitemaps exist today: static and dynamic.

      A static sitemap captures the URLs on your website at a particular point in time. The problem with this is that your site doesn’t stand still. 

      Publish a new page, remove an old one, change a URL, or redirect a page, and your static sitemap becomes outdated. That is, unless you regenerate it each time you make a change.

      However, a dynamic sitemap can keep up with these changes. It automatically updates as your site evolves, so search engines always get the most accurate view of the URLs currently live on your site. For most websites, this is the better choice.

      You don’t need to be an SEO expert to build a dynamic sitemap yourself. Many content management systems and website platforms can generate them for you.

      WordPress users can use plugins like Yoast SEO or Rank Math, while platforms like Shopify and Squarespace have built-in sitemap functionality.

articles.title: Tomorrow talked: A recap of Sprout’s 2026 Social Intelligence Summit
articles.fullContent:
When done successfully, social intelligence brings your day-to-day social data outside of the marketing silo and influences decisions made across the business. Sprout Social’s very first Social Intelligence Summit brought together industry leaders for a series of discussions focused on that idea, from spotting early signals to turning them into real business action.

Summit takeaways from across the sessions

  • Build permission before the moment you need it: Speed is blocked by approvals, so agree on guardrails, decision owners and a checklist in advance.
  • Relevance beats reactivity: Not every trend is right for every brand. Ask whether it fits, adds value and is something you can move on quickly before jumping in.
  • Social intelligence should change business decisions: The best stories turned conversation into action, like all-day breakfast and the Ziploc cereal bag or Dubai chocolate.
  • Translate for each stakeholder: Insights stall unless you frame them in the language and priorities of leadership, legal, product and other teams.
  • People are both the signal and the megaphone: Fans, ambassadors, employees and community managers are where signals start and where you can amplify your message.
  • Start small: For small teams, look to change things where you have influence.Take one signal to one team to achieve one outcome.
  • AI assists while humans decide: Use AI for summaries and efficiency, but keep a human in the loop and avoid content audiences recognize as AI-generated.

Here’s a deeper dive into the key takeaways from each session.

Keynote: How real-time social signals shape timing in marketing

Jay Schwedelson, founder of SubjectLine.com and CEO of Guru Media Hub, kicked off the summit with his keynote address on real-time social signals in marketing. His message was a blunt one; that marketing teams should stop guessing and start knowing. His agency runs around 40,000 campaigns every year, and he argued that your customers and your competitors’ customers are already telling you what you should do next. All social media marketers have to do is listen to them, then turn those insights into action faster than anyone else.

Social intelligence isn’t about collecting more data. It’s about actually making better decisions before anyone else does. Jay Schwedelson
CEO, Guru Media Hub

His first example focused on competitor complaints. Schwedelson suggested pulling the last 90 days of comments on three competitors’ posts and sorting them into buckets. Potential buckets included but weren’t limited to pricing, product failures and missing features. The next step is to pick a complaint your product solves or does better, and put out an us versus them post. The beauty of this is you don’t even have to name the competitor, if you’ve done your research correctly it’s something that people are already feeling, so they’ll naturally associate the negatives with the competitor. Though the origin of this is social, the profile of the people engaging are almost certainly already customers or considering buying, so this is mid-funnel or even lower-funnel work. Posting the same comparison on your website can also help with AI search, giving it a wider impact.

Timing was the second theme. When a platform launches a feature, it often gives a boost to the people who adopt it early. That means moving first can buy visibility. The same logic applies to culture. When a trend gets going, if you join a viral moment in the first 48 hours, your brand looks relevant; wait much longer than that and your brand looks behind. Citing Sprout’s 2026 Social Intelligence Report, Jay noted that only 10% of brands are able to act on an insight from social within hours, while 86% of organizations report missed opportunities because of delayed or siloed insights. His fix is a trend-to-campaign playbook with set guardrails and named decision owners. This ensures you don’t miss the moment while you’re still doing the rounds collecting approvals internally.

The critical thing in social media is moving at the speed of culture Jay Schwedelson
CEO, Guru Media Hub

He closed with two practical rules:

  1. Put paid budget behind posts that already work organically rather than trying to force success.
  2. Avoid generic AI-sounding language like “unlock”,”elevate” and “optimize”. Use the language your customers actually use instead.

First to know, first to move: Spotting cultural shifts before they become trends

Our first panel focused on the question social teams all over the world face every day; how do you tell a real cultural shift from a fleeting viral moment?

Moderator: Cat Anderson, Director of International Marketing, Sprout Social
Panelist: Josh Rangel, Senior Director of Social Strategy, Ogilvy
Panelist: Tulani André, VP of Social Content and Creator, Zolando

André encouraged audiences to focus less on the timing. Plenty of short-lived trends are still worth joining, so what matters is whether the moment and the trend itself fit with your brand, its goals and its voice. If it’s 24 hours later and there still isn’t an obvious on-ramp for you to join the conversation, then it probably isn’t for you.

I don’t think it’s the timing that kills it. I think it’s knowing if it’s right for your brand. Tulani André
VP of Social Content and Creator, Zalando

Rangel added that frameworks are your friend here. He recommended a checklist and an action plan that asks whether a trend is relevant, whether you can move quickly and whether you have something worth saying. Passing on one trend won’t cost the brand because there will always be another one. He also noted that approvals often stall with brand managers, legal and leadership. To avoid this, he advised educating those groups ahead of time, agreeing with legal on where the line is and showing leadership how trend work benefits the company in language they understand like sentiment and awareness.

What are Facebook analytics?

Facebook analytics are the performance data behind your Page, posts, and ads, covering how far your content travels, who sees it, and what they do next. The platform is used by 71% of U.S. adults. Think of analytics as the record of every interaction your brand earns on the platform, organized so you can spot patterns.

Most Facebook page analytics fall into a handful of categories:

  • Reach and impressions: How many people saw your content, and how many times it appeared.
  • Engagement: Reactions, comments, shares, saves, and clicks, usually summarized as an engagement rate.
  • Audience demographics: Age, gender, location, and language breakdowns for your followers.
  • Ad performance: Spend, cost per result, ROAS, and placement data from your paid campaigns. These metrics matter more as Meta’s average price per ad rose 9% in 2025.
  • Conversions: Link clicks, leads, purchases, and other actions tied back to your Facebook activity.

One note on naming: Facebook retired its standalone Facebook Analytics product in 2021 and folded reporting into Meta Business Suite. So when people say “Facebook Insights” today, they usually mean the Insights tab inside Business Suite.

Here’s where native Facebook insights typically run out of road:

  • No cross-platform view: You can see Facebook and Instagram, but not TikTok, LinkedIn, X, YouTube, or Pinterest alongside them.

Third-party tools solve for those gaps with a single facebook analytics dashboard, customizable reports, benchmarks, and in many cases social listening. “Click link in bio” is more than a meme; it’s also a revenue driver. When optimized, your Instagram link in bio turns casual views and engagements into measurable business outcomes.

What is an Instagram link in bio?

An Instagram link in bio is the clickable URL displayed in the bio section of your Instagram profile. Since the platform doesn’t let you add clickable links to your captions and comments, this is the only space where you can drive direct traffic to a specific website or page.

Source: Instagram

Until 2023, Instagram limited the number of bio links to one. Now you can add up to five clickable URLs in your bio.

Plus, you get access to comprehensive link analytics that show you exactly which campaigns worked and which ones fell flat. You can even tie your link performance to specific posts, helping you track what type of content generates clicks and conversions.

articles.title: How to Teach Content Strategy to Stakeholders Who Don’t Speak Marketing
articles.fullContent:
Key Takeaways

  • Content strategy buy-in often breaks down in translation to non-marketers, even when the strategy is sound.  
  • Lead with what your stakeholder already measures. How a strategy ties back to organizational cost, risk, or speed means more to them than marketing buzzwords. 
  • Call attention to problems or poor performance yourself. Clarify any wrong conclusions and present solutions before stakeholders have time to spiral. 
  • Name what stays the same before you name what changes, so new tactics feel familiar to your audience. 
  • General recommendations rarely get implemented. Give your audience specific action items in a portable checklist or one-pager. 

Most content strategies don’t fail on their merits. They stall out because content strategy buy-in never arrives from the person who funds the work, approves it, or executes part of it. That might be a client-side VP, your own executive team, a sales director, or a legal reviewer who has never opened your editorial calendar. 

The data supports the gap. Content Marketing Institute research ranks cross-department collaboration among the top content marketing challenges for 21 percent of B2B marketers. 

Content marketers get very good at doing the work but still struggle to convince stakeholders how necessary it is. Those are separate skills, and we need plenty of practice in both. 

If you feel like you’re failing to get the right stakeholders on side for your strategy, read on. You’ll learn how to explain content strategy to non-marketers, so they understand the rationale enough to defend it (even when you aren’t in the room). 

Teaching Is a Different Skill Than Doing

When stakeholders deny or ignore content strategy, we usually blame the audience. Leadership doesn’t get it. The client won’t listen. Sales ignored the brief (again). 

That explanation feels comfortable, but it’s not always the truth. The question is, how well are we explaining ourselves? 

The same pattern shows up in every department. A client executive, a product manager, and a compliance reviewer all evaluate your recommendation against a different set of priorities. A decision that looks obvious to a content strategist can read as a cost or a liability to someone who only thinks about content for 20 minutes a month. 

Stakeholder education in content marketing is a learnable skill, not a personality trait. Nobody is born knowing how to translate a content audit into CFO speak. You practice, watch what explanations tend to land, and adjust. Here’s what I’ve found works consistently. 

Start with the Stakes, Not the Solution

Lead with why the decision matters to the specific person in front of you, in their terms, before you name a framework or tactic. This does more for getting buy-in for content strategy than any deck you build. 

Attention follows relevance. Open with a scenario that matches your stakeholder’s priorities, then connect your recommendation to it. 

Use this same move across different audiences: 

  • A budget holder hears a content refresh as spend on something already done. Reframe it as efficiency. You’re reinvesting in assets that already earn traffic instead of funding net-new pages that take months to mature.  
  • Legal hears a byline requirement on articles as more review work eating up their time. Reframe it as attribution control. Named authors with verifiable credentials reduce the risk of unsourced claims attributed to the company. 
  • Sales hears a webpage restructure as a cosmetic change. Reframe it as speed. Clear subheads and direct answers let a rep send one link mid-deal instead of writing a custom explanation. 

Translate your content strategy into the currency your audience already trades in, then explain the specifics where you need sign-off. Most collaborators tune in if you’re covering cost, risk, or speed. 

Beyond buzzwords, root your argument in data they recognize. A content strategist lives in organic sessions, keyword rankings, and time on page. A sales leader watches pipeline contribution and deal velocity; a CFO watches customer acquisition cost and ROI. You don’t have to drop your own metrics, just connect them. Bring the organic sessions that became pipeline; tie your rankings to the deals they influenced. Pull evidence from the dashboard they already open, then draw the line from your metric to theirs. 

Defuse the Scariest Interpretation Before They Invent It

Nearly every content strategy shift arrives attached to an alarming headline. A traffic decline. A ranking drop. A platform change nobody controls. 

The Pew Research Center tracked 68,879 Google searches and found click-through fell from 15% to 8% when an AI Overview appeared. Read that insight cold in a quarterly review and your client hears one message: our investment is evaporating. 

Speak to those concerns before they raise them. State the numbers plainly, then correct potential wrong conclusions immediately. Something like this works: “organic clicks are getting harder to win on informational queries as search engine trends shift, which is why we’re moving effort toward pages that convert and toward becoming the source these systems cite.” 

Skipping an uncomfortable number doesn’t make it disappear. Your audience fills in the blank themselves, usually with something worse than reality, and you find out during Q&A after you’ve lost the floor.

articles.fullContent:
For brands, social media is a goldmine of real-time insight into consumers’ preferences, behaviors and motivations. And segmenting social users intentionally—using live conversation data rather than static demographic details—empowers leaders to make smarter business decisions, whether it’s optimizing spend, discovering new markets or driving revenue.

But social media audience segmentation isn’t a one‑off marketing exercise. It’s a dynamic, cyclical process designed to spot emerging opportunities and inform data-grounded strategies.

With the help of this guide, you can better understand how to approach social media audience segmentation and use it to make an impact across the business.

What is social media audience segmentation?

Social media audience segmentation is the process of breaking down your target audience that’s engaging on social networks into smaller, distinct groups based on shared characteristics, behaviors or interests.

In contrast to broader marketing segmentation, social segmentation draws on real-time social data. Think live conversation, engagement and sentiment data, rather than CRM or survey inputs that may reflect the past and not a user’s present feelings.

Segmentation is one of the many pillars of social media intelligence, helping organizations move beyond broad audience assumptions by uncovering the distinct groups driving conversations online. Teams can then make more targeted decisions aligned to the current pulse of the market across customer care, product innovation, campaign planning and overall business strategy.

Why audience segmentation matters more than ever

One of the key factors driving the need for segmentation is the degradation of trust and attention among consumers.

According to the Q1 2026 Sprout Pulse Survey, consumers are becoming more particular about what they engage with online, with two-thirds (66%) feeling more selective than a year ago. AI slop (i.e. undifferentiated, one-size-fits-all content) was cited as a contributor to eroding trust; 56% of respondents said they see AI slop often or very often.

Many brands are mistakenly investing in this generic content. This ultimately results in wasted budget as platforms are increasingly rewarding relevance over reach.

Segmentation is what enables brands to achieve personalization and, in turn, resonance with their audiences—without necessarily needing to increase headcount or budget.

4 types of social media audience segments (and where social data fits)

Let’s take a look at four key types of social media audience segments, what they tell you and the social signals that paint the picture of who they are.

Demographic segmentation

Basic demographics like age, gender or follower count are a reasonable starting point in creating social media segments. This data is garnered via self-disclosure (i.e. a user inputs this information when creating a profile), network-level audience demographics reported by ad managers or analytics tools.

While these details don’t tell you much on their own, they can reveal behavioral trends. For instance, you may see a generational skew depending on the networks and content formats a person engages with. In general, Instagram Reels and TikToks attract a younger audience, while Facebook’s most active users skew older.

However, it’s important to note that demographics don’t provide the soundest basis for segmentation because the data is often self-reported. Users may skip fields or deliberately enter false details to protect their privacy or access age-restricted content.

Demographic-based targeting is also losing its predictive power. Per the 2026 Influencer Marketing Report, only 17% of consumers check follower count before following a creator. For nearly half of respondents (47%), things like content topic and behavior matter far more.

With that in mind, demographics should be used as a starting point rather than a primary segmentation driver. Instead of examining people’s surface-level traits, look at the things they say and do unprompted on social. These signals are more dynamic and indicative of how people identify themselves.

Psychographic segmentation

Psychographics is the classification of people based on psychological criteria—such as values, attitudes or motivations—that influence their engagement and consumption patterns.

To segment your social audience by psychographics, review their comments, posts and shares. The content they post or engage with can tell you a lot about their internal beliefs. Your brand can then use these insights to tailor its content and target these users more closely.

For example, if your audience members regularly post about climate change and sustainability, you can place them into an environmentally motivated segment. From there, you can center your messaging around subjects related to your brand, like ethically sourced materials, reusable products or community initiatives.

Behavioral segmentation on social

While psychographics focus on what users believe, behavioral segmentation shines a light on how they behave on social. The actions they take, the conversations they partake in and the content formats they engage with.

To build behavioral segments, brands must observe audiences’ patterns. How often do they post? What formats do they share (e.g. static images, carousels, Reels)? What are they talking about in comment sections? Whose posts are they commenting on?

Finding the answers to these questions can unearth important information about consumers’ decision-making and motivations. In addition to seeing how people behave, you’ll begin to understand why. You won’t just see who they interact with, but who they really are behind the screen.

Say you identify a segment of users consistently participating in giveaways, promo codes and engaging with shopping-on-a-budget content. With this data, you can glean what might be most important to them when making purchase decisions: fair pricing and discount offers. From there, you can tailor your social messaging accordingly, whether it’s highlighting affordable prices or sharing the outsized value of your offerings.

Geographic segmentation

A person’s physical location shapes their social and spending habits—and the two often go hand in hand.

Various social signals enable brands to glean a user’s whereabouts, including location tags, geotagged posts and stories, and the language or dialect they use on social. Additionally, some network behaviors and preferences are region-specific.

Key Takeaways

  • The 4 Ps (product, price, place, and promotion) are tools marketers use in combination to shape how a product (or range of products) is positioned, promoted, and sold to a specific group of customers. Together, they’re often referred to as the “marketing mix.”

  • Well-known companies like Rolex, McDonald’s, and Red Bull have perfected the 4 Ps behind their products and brand identities.
  • AI is changing how marketers execute the 4 Ps, but the fundamental questions behind product, price, place, and promotion remain the same.

The 4 Ps of marketing (product, price, place, and promotion) have been around for decades, and they still drive decisions around every successful product launch.

Also known as the “marketing mix,” they help you think through how to bring a product to market and reach the customers most likely to buy it.

It doesn’t matter if you’re running a one-person small business or a global enterprise. The 4 Ps help you bring a product to market and get it in front of people most likely to buy it.

How you put the 4 Ps to work has changed, though. AI is giving marketers new ways to understand their customers and make more informed decisions, often in less time.

I’ll cover some of these opportunities as I show you how the 4 Ps still drive marketing decision-making today.

What Are the Four Elements of the Marketing Mix?

The 4 Ps of marketing, commonly known as the marketing mix, stand for product, place, price, and promotion. They’re like four levers companies can adjust to better position their products for the customers they want to reach.

Here’s the meaning behind each of the four Ps: 

  • Product: What you’re selling, including its features, packaging, and the support that comes with it
  • Price: What you charge and how you structure the pricing
  • Place: Where and how your customers can buy the product
  • Promotion: How you get the word out about the product

To more fully understand the 4 Ps of advertising, we need to take a step back. Mention “marketing,” and most people think of customer-facing content like ads, social media posts, emails, videos, and blog articles like this one. 

In fact, these represent just one piece of a much broader discipline. They’re the “promotion” part of the mix called marketing communications.

True marketing is a big-picture process that strives to meet all customer needs. And thinking in terms of the 4 Ps allows companies to do exactly that. 

What About the 7 Ps and the 4 Cs?

The idea of a marketing mix has been around longer than the 4 Ps themselves.

In 1948, Harvard professor James Culliton described marketing executives as “mixer(s) of ingredients.” Inspired by this idea, fellow Harvard professor Neil Borden often referred to the concept of the marketing mix in the years that followed. 

Then in 1960, marketing professor E. Jerome McCarthy organized it into the four elements we know today in his book Basic Marketing: A Managerial Approach.

Other models have been suggested in the years since, with two in particular gaining traction: the 7 Ps and the 4 Cs:

  • The 7 Ps: In 1981, marketing professors Bernard Booms and Mary Jo Bitner expanded the 4 Ps to better suit service-based businesses. Their model adds people, process, and physical evidence to the mix. These cover the employees who deliver a service, the delivery process, and the environment where business takes place. 
  • The 4 Cs: Marketing professor Robert Lauterborn proposed a more customer-oriented alternative to the 4 Ps in 1990. His model replaces them with consumer wants and needs, cost, convenience, and communication. Instead of starting with what a business wants to sell, the 4 Cs push marketers to focus on what customers actually need. 

These alternative models add some useful nuance. To me, though, the 4 Ps still make up the strongest foundation for marketing campaigns.
